welcome.heading: Welcome to the Market
welcome.body: Before charts. Before setups. Before Dayli ICC. You need to understand the world you're stepping into. In this section, we're breaking trading down from the ground up — what you're actually buying and selling, why price moves, what a futures contract is, and how movement on your chart translates into real dollars. No strategy yet. No entries yet. First, we're learning the language.
welcome.mission: Don't memorize trading terms. Understand what they mean.

challenge.title: Know What You're Trading
challenge.subtitle: This isn't the Knowledge Check. It's a quick, interactive competency check.

rounds.heading: Round 1 — What are you doing?
rounds.prompt: You expect price to decline and want to participate in that move.
rounds.question: Long or short?

options.label: Short
options.feedback: Right — short is the position that benefits when price falls.

options.label: Long
options.feedback: Long benefits from price rising — not what you want if you expect a decline.

options.label: Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100
options.feedback: Exactly — MNQ is the micro version of the Nasdaq-100 futures contract.

options.label: E-mini Nasdaq-100
options.feedback: That's NQ — the full-size version. MNQ is the micro.

options.label: Micro Gold
options.feedback: That's MGC, a different market entirely.

rounds.heading: Round 3 — Spot the problem
rounds.prompt: A friend tells you she made "50 points today."
rounds.question: Do you know how much money she made?

options.label: No — you don't know the instrument or contract count
options.feedback: Right — points alone don't tell you anything about dollars without the instrument and size.

options.label: Yes — 50 points is 50 points
options.feedback: Points alone can't tell you a dollar amount.

options.label: Yes, if she's trading MNQ
options.feedback: Even on MNQ, you'd still need to know her contract count.
That's only 1 contract's worth — you have 2.
That's just the points, not multiplied by point value or contracts.

rounds.heading: Round 5 — Think like a trader
rounds.prompt: A trader says: "I'm bullish, so I'm entering."
rounds.question: What's missing from that decision? Select everything that applies.
rounds.successFeedback: Exactly. Direction alone isn't a trading plan.

questionBank.question: What is trading, at its core?
options: Participating in a market by taking a position based on the expectation that price will move
Predicting the future with certainty
Owning a company
questionBank.why: Trading is participation based on expectation — not certainty.

questionBank.question: A trader takes a position designed to profit if price falls. What is that called?
options: Short
Long
Hedge
questionBank.why: Short positions benefit when price falls.

questionBank.question: What creates a market?
options: Buyers and sellers with different opinions transacting
The exchange setting a price
One trader deciding the price
questionBank.why: Disagreement between participants is what creates a transaction.

questionBank.question: A producer uses futures to manage exposure to changing prices. What is that called?
options: Hedging
Speculating
Investing
questionBank.why: Hedging is using futures to manage risk, not to speculate on direction.

questionBank.question: Does a single green candle prove buyers control the whole market?
options: No — one candle doesn't tell the larger structural story
Yes — green always means bullish control
Only if it's a large candle
questionBank.why: Context matters more than any single candle.

questionBank.question: What is a futures contract?
options: A standardized agreement whose value moves with an underlying asset or benchmark
A share of ownership in a company
A savings account
questionBank.why: Futures contracts track price movement, not ownership.

questionBank.question: What does MNQ represent?
options: Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100
E-mini Nasdaq-100
Micro Gold
questionBank.why: MNQ is the micro version of the Nasdaq-100 futures contract.

questionBank.question: What's the relationship between NQ and MNQ?
options: MNQ is 1/10th the contract multiplier of NQ
They're the exact same contract size
NQ is the micro version of MNQ
questionBank.why: MNQ is the smaller, micro version of NQ.

questionBank.question: Which is true about futures contracts, unlike stocks?
options: Futures contracts expire and can require a rollover
Futures never expire
Futures are a form of company ownership
questionBank.why: Futures have expiration and rollover — stocks don't.

questionBank.question: Maya trades 10 shares of a stock, then decides to trade 10 MNQ contracts because "10 is her normal size." What's wrong?
options: Share count and contract count aren't equivalent units of risk
Nothing — 10 is always 10
MNQ contracts are always smaller risk than shares
questionBank.why: The same number can carry very different dollar risk depending on the instrument.

questionBank.question: On MNQ, what is one point worth per contract?
questionBank.why: MNQ's minimum tick is 0.25 points worth $0.50, so a full point is $2 per contract.

questionBank.question: You buy 1 MNQ at 20,000 and price rises to 20,010. What's the P&L before fees?
A trader says "I only have a 30-point stop, so I can't lose much." What's missing from that statement?
options: The number of contracts and the contract's point value
Nothing — the statement is complete
Her broker's name
questionBank.why: Points alone don't establish dollar risk without contract count and point value.

questionBank.question: Why is "I think price is going up" not a complete trading plan?
options: It doesn't define entry, risk, invalidation, target, or confirmation
It's actually a complete plan on its own
Because direction can never be known
questionBank.why: A real plan needs more than a directional opinion.

questionBank.question: What is the P&L formula?
options: Points moved × point value × contract count
Points moved ÷ contract count
Entry price × exit price
questionBank.why: All three pieces are needed to turn a point move into a real dollar result.

questionBank.question: A trader's thesis supports higher prices, but price moves against her. What's the AGHF mindset?
options: A thesis can be reasonable and still be wrong — risk defines what happens next
The analysis must eventually become correct
She should add to the position to average in
questionBank.why: Being reasonable and being right aren't the same — that's exactly why risk is defined in advance.

prompts.whatClicked: In your own words, what is trading?
prompts.didntKnow: One thing I didn't know before this section:
prompts.explainToFriend: Your friend asks: "Okay...but what exactly am I buying when I trade MNQ?" Explain it to her in your own words.
